Statement in opposition to
L.D. 172, An Act to Require the Maine State Police to Create a Statewide List of Missing Persons
Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
February 3, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and honorable members of the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee. My name is Jason Moen. I am the Chief of the Auburn Police Department and serve as President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association. I am submitting testimony on behalf of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association in opposition to LD 172.
The Mission of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association is to secure a closer official and personal relationship among Maine Police Officials; to secure a unity of action in law enforcement matters; to enhance the standards of police personnel, police training and police professionalism generally; to devise ways and means for equality of law enforcement throughout the state of Maine; to advance the prevention and detection of crime; to prescribe to the Law Enforcement Code of Ethics; and to promote the profession of law enforcement as an integral and dedicated force in today's society sworn to the protection of life and property.
As proposed, the Bureau of State Police shall establish and maintain a publicly accessible website that lists all open missing person cases in Maine. The website must contain a summary of the details of each individual case, a picture of the missing person and the contact information for the investigating agency of that case.

Our opposition is not based on maintaining a public list of open missing person cases. Quite the contrary. We support the law that is currently on the books that requires all Maine law enforcement officers to report all missing persons to the state's Chief Medical Examiner's Office. As described in the testimony provided by the Maine State Police, that information is entered into a national database that the public can access on the US Department of Justice's website. This system has provided law enforcement agencies a powerful and effective system to help solve cases well beyond our state's borders.
It does not make sense to duplicate a system that is already in place that meets the objective of this legislation, especially when that effort would come at a significant cost to the state. As policymakers and public safety officials, we can collectively do a better job of educating the public of the NamUs website (Home | NamUs). This free and easy-to-use dashboard provides law enforcement, medical examiners and families of missing persons access to information to help resolve open cases.
On behalf of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association, we respectfully ask that the Committee vote Ought Not to Pass on LD 172.

Re: LD 172 -- An Act to Require the Maine State Police to Create a Statewide List of Missing Persons
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and members of the committee,

I am Lindsey Chasteen, the Office Administrator for the Office of Chief Medical Examiner (OCME). I
am speaking neither for nor against LD 172 today. My testimony should be viewed as merely
informational. As of 1991, the Office of Chief Medical Examiner has been statutorily tasked with being the State Clearinghouse for Maine's missing people.

Per statute, being the State Clearinghouse means my agency is responsible for maintaining files on missing
persons sufficient for the purpose of identification when there is reason to suspect that those persons may
not be found alive. As of today, the OCME has 148 missing people on our radar. The oldest disappearance is from 1947. The OCME uses a publicly accessible website, run by the National Institute of Justice as
our case management system.

This website is the National Missing and Unidentified Person System (NamUs), and provides basic information such as a photo, circumstances, and the investigative agency information to the public, while
keeping the biometric information (fingerprint classification, medical and DNA information) private and
only viewable by case contributors. Case contributors are staff at the OCME, and the assigned law
enforcement agency.
Over the years, there has been discussion between the OCME and Maine State Police about whether the
Maine State Police should list all Maine's missing people on their website. In response to these
discussions, and in an attempt to provide the public with more information, several years ago the OCME
updated our agency webpage to include a link to NamUs and an explanation that we are the State
Clearinghouse. Our webpage is housed within the Office of the Attorney General website.
Even though the OCME is only an agency of 12 people, and we handle over 2,000 death investigations a
year, we know our missing people by name and review their case files regularly.

Thank you for your time.

Lindsey Chasteen, MBA

Testimony ofRepresentative Nina Milliken presenting
LD 172, An Act to Require the Maine State Police to Create a Statewide List of Missing Persons
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
Hello Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and friends and colleagues on the best committee in the
Maine Legislature, Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Nina Milliken and I am honored to represent
the people of the towns of Blue Hill, Brooksville, Castine, Sedgwick, Surry and Trenton in the Maine House. I
am happy to be here today to present to you LD 172, An Act to Require the Maine State Police to Create a
Statewide List of Missing Persons.
This bill is a simple bill, the title of the bill is only about half as long as the language of the bill itself. It requires that the State Police, in cooperation with all law enforcement agencies across the state, maintain a publicly available list of all missing persons in the state. Currently, if a person goes missing in Bangor, for example, that person would be listed as a missing person through Bangor Police Department. If a person goes missing in
Lewiston, they'd be listed with Lewiston Police. And if a person goes missing in my small town of Blue Hill, it
would depend on when they went missing, as they could be listed under Hancock County Sheriff 's Office or Maine State Police depending on the day. This, of course, means that the State Police has and maintains a list of
missing persons. But this list is not the entire list of missing persons in Maine. It is simply the list of persons
who went missing where the state police was the agency of jurisdiction, or where the agency of jurisdiction
handed the case over to the state police.
While this may be how it has always been done or how it has been done for some time, families of missing persons who believe their loved one could be anywhere in Maine would like to see an easily accessible list of all
missing persons in Maine that is in one, concise location. I would imagine it feels harmful to look at the Maine
State Police's list of missing persons and not see your loved one who went missing in a place with a municipal department. Additionally, we live in an age of social media and intemet detective work. Online sleuths want an easy to access and complete list. And, as we don't have a great system for alerting the public to missing persons (billboards are prohibited and milk cartons are no longer a popular option), it feels prudent that we use whatever tools we have available to help these families find their loved ones as quickly as possible.
I might suggest a slight amendment to the bill to require that, in addition to creating and maintaining the list, there be some attempt made to regularly notify the public when a new person is added to the list and to update
as time goes on. In September, a young woman from New Sweden named Stefanie Damron went missing. It
would be useful, I think, for the public to be reminded of her case and shown her image every month or more so
we all continue to look for her.

TO: JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON CRIMINAL JUSTICE AND PUBLIC SAFETY FROM: TAMMY LACHER SCULLY, BELFAST ME
Sen. Beebe-Center, Rep. Hasenfus & Members of the Committee: l am here to speak in support
of LD 172.
The nightmare l've been living since June 6, 2022--when my disabled adult son Graham Lacher went
missing from DDPC in Bangor--could be told in numbers. 974: the number of days he's been lost to us;
72: the number of hours experts say you have before the chances of finding a missing person go way
down; 120: the number of hours authorities waited before conducting a thorough search for my son;
ZERO: the number of confirmed sightings we've had of Graham since he disappeared.
Members of the public are often surprised that we still haven't found him. but, as members of this
committee, it probably does not surprise you. Because, as you likely know:
- there is no official ongoing search for Graham & there hasn't been since 30 days after he disappeared 5 - there was never a true, systemwide alert associated with his disappearance; - nor is there any consistent protocol for following up on possible leads when someone thinks they have
seen him.
I can provide supporting details on these points if you'd like, but in brief: It took several, precious hours
to get the Bangor PD to issue a Silver Alert (hours in which the public was coming home from work or going out for the evening and might have seen him). The alert, once issued, was heartbreakingly limited in scope. (it was not sent to first responders, hospital emergency departments, or any of the service providers Graham might encounter as a homeless person. And, as you know, Silver Alerts are not transmitted via the emergency alert system.) It even took me months just to get the Dept. of Public Safety to correct all of the misleading/false information contained in the Silver Alert that was issued.
The bottom line: ln Maine, there is no official understanding of what to do or when to do it when someone like my son goes missing.
To make up for this, we've done everything we can think of to inform the public ourselves. Among other
things: We held informational rallies in Maine's major cities; sent posters to every tagging station in
Maine to alert hunters; notified every library; placed road signs throughout the state; attempted our own
version of a regional alert in case he crossed state borders; asked convenience stores throughout the state to display his photo after the lottery commission took him off their screens; provided vehicle magnets to anyone willing to raise awareness that way; asked businesses to put post-it notes on
customer orders & sent 1,000 postcards to all the places that should have been contacted in the first place, and, for good measure, included every state legislator, commissioner, the attorney general & the
governor.
But l am here today because, after two and a half years, my son is not even listed by the Department of
Public Safety on Maine's missing persons list.
Why is this important? For one thing: Despite all our efforts & the hundreds of ordinary citizens who have helped us, we are regularly asked if we are running a scam--because when people google "missing people in Maine," Graham's name is not on the official list. If peopie don't know he's missingor don't believe that he's missing--how will we ever find him? Not publicly listing our missing loved ones sends the message that Maine does not care if they are found. lt also hinders researchers & iournallsts
from measuring the scope of the problems related to missing person cases.
Our family has logged many thousands of miles and spent many thousands of dollars trying to raise public awareness. Despite our efforts, we still find that most people we encounter on our travels have not heard of my son Graham. Maine can do better by families like mine. Passing this bill, honestly, is the
least that you can do.

An Act to Require the Maine State Police to Create a Statewide List of Missing Persons
Sponsored by Rep. Milliken Joint Standing Committee on Criminal justice and Public Safety

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and other distinguished members of the joint standing
committee on Criminal ]ustice and Public Safety. My name is Lieutenant Thomas Pickering and I am here
representing the Maine State Police and the Maine Department of Public Safety and to testify in
OPPOSITION to LD 172.

Current Maine Law (Title 22 SS 3034) requires all Maine Law Enforcement to report all missing persons to
the Maine Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. Currently, no requirement exists to report all missing persons to the Maine State Police. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner currently enters those missing
person into NAMUS (National Missing and Unidentified Persons System). The website is an official website
of the United States Government, Department of Justice. This public website exists to cross reference missing persons in one jurisdiction with recovered remains from another jurisdiction. The website is a very effective tool for making connections between the missing person from Maine and the recovered remains
from California as an example. This website is a public list.

Between 2015 and 2018, the Maine State Police and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner worked diligently to reconcile missing persons cases between the two offices and to obtain biological samples from those next of kin in the event that potential remains are recovered. Several members of the Major Crimes Unit were part of that effort along with several at the Medical Examiner's Office. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner continues to be the official repository in Maine for keeping this list because of their obvious connection to the recovery of remains within the state and the statutory mandate for reporting to
them.

There is a link from the Chief Medical Examiner's website to the NAMUS website, which can be accessed by
any inquiring party. Though this list is not on a Maine.gov website it is a published list of Maine missing persons. The easiest way forward would be for any published list to exist on the Chief Medical Examiner's Maine.gov website. I have spoken with Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in the past and they would need to hire additional administrative support to support a missing persons list published on their
Maine. gov website.
